title: Model Context Protocol
subtitle: One protocol, not M times N integrations

slides.title: The problem: M times N integrations
bullets: M AI apps x N tools/data sources = up to M x N bespoke integrations
Each one hand-built, each with its own auth, schema, error conventions
Every new tool means every AI app re-implements the same adapter
This is the exact shape USB and LSP already solved elsewhere
slides.notes: Ask the room: how many custom Slack/DB/Drive integrations has their org built for different AI tools already? Usually more than one.

slides.title: The USB-C analogy
slides.quote: MCP is like a USB-C port for AI applications.
bullets: One interface for tool/data builders to target
One client implementation for AI apps to support
Anthropic open-sourced it November 2024; now community-governed
slides.notes: This is the spec's own framing, not a stretch analogy. Also compare to LSP for editors/languages.

slides.title: What MCP does NOT solve
bullets: It standardizes the WIRE CONTRACT, not the integration work itself
Someone still writes the adapter mapping a tool to your backend
Someone still decides scope: what should a model be ALLOWED to do
MCP relocates integration work to be reusable -- it doesn't remove it
slides.notes: Set expectations early. MCP is not magic; it's a standard interface, same as REST didn't eliminate backend logic.

slides.title: Three primitives, three control loci
slides.notes: This table is the single most important idea in the whole module. Everything else is mechanics.

slides.title: The most common MCP design mistake
bullets: Putting a pure data-fetch behind a Tool
-> model must DECIDE to fetch context that should just be there
Putting a side-effecting action behind a Resource
-> nothing stops a host from silently loading it into every chat
Ask: who should decide when this runs? That answer picks the primitive
slides.notes: Give a concrete example: 'read this file' as a tool wastes a model turn. 'send this email' as a resource is a silent-execution bug.

slides.title: Tool descriptions are not documentation
bullets: The model reads name + description + JSON Schema to decide when/how to call
Vague verbs (process, handle) make the model guess
State exact semantics: 'case-insensitive substring match', not 'searches'
SDK builds the schema FROM your type hints -- no drift to keep in sync
slides.notes: Live demo: open minimal_mcp_server.py and read search_catalog's docstring aloud as if you were the model.

slides.title: Error handling: the bug everyone writes once
bullets: raise ToolError(...) -> result with is_error=True, model can retry
return "error message" -> is_error=False, looks like SUCCESS
Every client UI and the model itself reads is_error to route logic
Resources are stricter: a miss is a protocol-level error, no in-between
slides.notes: Run code/mcp_client_demo.py's failed search_catalog call live and point at is_error=True in the printed JSON.

slides.title: Architecture and wire protocol
slides.subtitle: Host, Client, Server, and what's actually on the wire

slides.title: Host, Client, Server
bullets: HOST: the AI application a human uses (Claude Desktop, an IDE, your agent)
CLIENT: one per server connection, maintained by the host
SERVER: implements tools/resources/prompts against a real backend
5 servers connected = 5 client objects, each blind to the others
Cross-server coordination is the HOST's job, not the protocol's
slides.notes: Draw the 1:1 client-server pairing on the board. This is why agents federating many servers need their own orchestration logic.

slides.title: Transports: local vs remote
rows: Client spawns server as subprocess; JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout
slides.notes: Older HTTP+SSE (two endpoints) was replaced by Streamable HTTP in 2025-03-26. Flag it as deprecated if it shows up in old tutorials.

slides.title: Every message is JSON-RPC 2.0
bullets: Request: jsonrpc, id, method, params
Response: jsonrpc, id, and result OR error
Notification: no id, no reply expected
SDK pydantic models ARE this JSON, just deserialized -- not a simulation
slides.notes: model_dump(mode='json') on any SDK object reproduces the wire payload exactly. Show this in mcp_client_demo.py's show() helper.

slides.title: The classic handshake (2024-11-05 through 2025-11-25)
bullets: 1. Client sends initialize: protocolVersion, capabilities, clientInfo
2. Server replies with its own version, capabilities, serverInfo
3. Client sends notifications/initialized -- one-way, no reply
Session now in Operation phase; tools/list, tools/call, etc. flow
This is what virtually every deployed server speaks TODAY
slides.notes: This is what mcp_client_demo.py performs and prints. The negotiated version in the demo is 2025-11-25.

slides.title: 2026-07-28: the stateless redesign
bullets: Handshake removed entirely -- no initialize/initialized at all
Every request carries protocolVersion + capabilities in _meta
Discovery becomes one optional call: server/discover
List results now cacheable via ttlMs / cacheScope fields
Sampling and logging (client primitives) marked deprecated
slides.notes: This is the CURRENT spec as of writing, but adoption is nascent. SDKs remain dual-era and still speak the classic handshake by default.

slides.title: Trust, security, and where MCP fits
slides.subtitle: An MCP server is code you didn't write, running with privileges you granted

slides.title: The trust model, stated plainly
bullets: An MCP server is a DEPENDENCY, not just a data source
Local stdio server = runs with YOUR os-user privileges
Tool output is untrusted input the model can't distinguish from the user
Vet a server like a new prod dependency: what can it READ, WRITE, TRIGGER
slides.notes: Connect directly to Module 13's lethal trifecta: untrusted input + sensitive access + exfil channel.

slides.title: Named attacks from the spec's security guidance
rows: Static client ID + consent cookie skips user consent
Server forwards a token not issued for it
Malicious server points OAuth discovery at internal IPs
Stateless server doesn't bind handle to caller
slides.notes: These are documented, named attack classes in the spec's own security_best_practices doc -- not hypothetical.

slides.title: Independent research backs the trust framing
bullets: 67,057 servers audited across 6 registries -- widespread hijack conditions found
1,899 open-source servers: 8 vuln classes, only 3 overlap traditional CWEs
Tool poisoning: malicious instructions in a tool's OWN description
The attack surface is what a tool claims, not just what it returns
slides.notes: Cite papers/PAPERS.md arXiv:2510.16558, 2506.13538, 2603.22489. Numbers will be stale -- the categories won't.

slides.title: MCP vs. the alternatives
rows: Overkill inside one system you own
slides.notes: The line to land: MCP is how an agent gets a screwdriver; A2A is how it asks another agent to build the shelf.

slides.title: Governance: a server is a new vendor
bullets: Map what it reads and what it writes/triggers BEFORE approval
Prefer registry-listed, verified-namespace servers over random repo URLs
Scope credentials to least privilege -- no admin key for convenience
Log tool calls like any privileged API call for audit reconstruction
slides.notes: This is the same vendor-risk lens Module 12 applies to any third-party dependency. MCP doesn't invent a new category.

slides.title: Exit check
bullets: Run mcp_client_demo.py end to end; read every printed JSON message
Explain why the failed search_catalog call is is_error=True, not a protocol error
Name the primitive you'd use for a new hypothetical tool, with a control-locus reason
State one concrete trust decision before connecting a third-party server
